decision.ambiguity_note: Several concrete ambiguities and dataset-shift risks are present. (1) Label ambiguity: 'debris' is not a standard histological entity and overlaps heavily with 'mucus' and 'background' in H&E appearance; 'background' is a catch-all for non-tissue or artifact regions; 'cancer-associated stroma' and 'smooth muscle' can be visually indistinguishable at patch level without architectural context; 'normal colon mucosa' vs. 'colorectal adenocarcinoma epithelium' has a dysplastic transition zone that is inherently ambiguous at the 96×96 patch resolution used in PathMNIST. (2) Distribution shift: train and val class proportions are nearly identical (max |Δ| < 0.001), but the test set (CRC-VAL-HE-7K, different clinical center) deviates substantially—adipose prevalence nearly doubles (10.4%→18.6%, ratio 1.79), mucus rises (8.9%→14.4%, ratio 1.62), while debris drops sharply (11.5%→4.7%, ratio 0.41), cancer-associated stroma drops (10.4%→5.9%, ratio 0.56), and smooth muscle drops (13.5%→8.2%, ratio 0.61). This is not a random sampling artifact; it reflects a different tissue-sampling or slide-preparation protocol at the external center. (3) Domain shift: the test set explicitly originates from a different clinical center, introducing uncontrolled variation in H&E staining intensity/hue, scanner color calibration, slide thickness, and fixation quality. The 'debris' class collapse (ratio 0.41) is consistent with different slide-preparation or scanning artifacts at the new site, meaning the model's learned 'debris' features may not transfer. (4) The test set is also smaller (7,180 vs. 89,996 train), amplifying the statistical impact of the skewed distribution and reducing per-class test samples for the under-represented classes (debris n=339, cancer-associated stroma n=421, smooth muscle n=592), making per-class test metrics noisy and less reliable. (5) No information is provided about whether the external center used the same annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, or whether 'debris' and 'background' were defined identically, compounding the label-ambiguity risk under domain shift.

'Cancer-associated stroma' vs. 'smooth muscle' and 'normal colon mucosa' vs. 'adenocarcinoma epithelium' are inherently ambiguous at 96×96 patch resolution without multi-scale architectural context, increasing misclassification risk under domain shift.

The near-identical train/val split (max proportion difference <0.001) suggests a random split of a single-site dataset, meaning the only true external generalization test is the skewed CRC-VAL-HE-7K set, which conflates distribution shift with domain shift.

Patch-level classification without spatial context means the model cannot leverage tissue architecture to disambiguate stroma from smooth muscle or dysplastic from normal epithelium, a limitation that is exacerbated when staining appearance shifts across centers.

decision.rationale:
The channel statistics (means ≈ 0.53–0.74, stds ≈ 0.12–0.18) indicate the 28×28 H&E patches are already in a [0,1] pixel range but are not zero-centered and have low, uneven variance across channels. Applying 'standardize' (zero-mean, unit-variance per channel) equalizes the scale of the three H&E channels and centers the distribution, which improves gradient conditioning for a small-resolution classifier and prevents the higher-mean channels (R, B) from dominating early training over the lower-mean G channel. 'unit' scaling would leave the data off-center and with unequal per-channel magnitudes, offering no numerical benefit over the raw [0,1] input.

For augmentations (train-only, per design_evidence), I selected three that address the two dominant sources of variability in H&E tissue-type classification at 28×28: (1) spatial orientation and (2) staining photometry. hflip and vflip are both orientation-safe for tissue-type labels (tissue micro-architecture has no inherent left-right or up-down axis) and together they generate four effective orientations, doubling the spatial diversity of the ~90k training patches without introducing unrealistic geometry. brightness is the single most impactful photometric augmentation for H&E because inter-lab and inter-slide staining intensity shifts primarily manifest as a global multiplicative/additive change in pixel values; modeling this invariance reduces the model's reliance on absolute color and improves generalization across the 9 tissue classes. I deliberately omitted rotate90 (redundant coverage already provided by the flip pair) and contrast (less dominant than brightness for H&E variability, and at 28×28 aggressive contrast shifts risk destroying the fine texture cues that distinguish the 9 classes). The moderate class imbalance (ratio 1.63) does not require additional augmentation to compensate, so the budget of 3 is best spent on the highest-leverage transforms above.

decision.analysis: The task operates on 28×28×3 images with ~90k training samples and a moderate class imbalance (1.63×). Three architectural facts dominate the design space. (1) Spatial resolution is extremely small: a 7×7 stride-2 first convolution (as in resnet18) immediately collapses 28→14→7, leaving only 49 spatial positions after the first block, which wastes the deeper layers' capacity. (2) Channel statistics are highly asymmetric—means range from 0.53 to 0.74 and stds from 0.12 to 0.18—so per-channel normalisation is not optional; it is the single highest-leverage preprocessing step. The low overall variance (all stds < 0.18) implies that discriminative signal is subtle and concentrated, favouring architectures with strong local feature extraction and careful normalisation over architectures that rely on global context from the outset. (3) The dataset size (~90k) is comfortable for CNNs but tight for full-scale transformers, especially given the imbalance which effectively reduces the minority-class sample count. Architecture ranking: residual_cnn is the strongest default because 2–4 residual blocks with 32→64→128 channels exploit local structure at 28×28 without over-parameterisation, and skip connections stabilise training at this depth. tiny_cnn serves as a fast, low-risk baseline for hyperparameter sweeps. compact_transformer is the preferred transformer entry point: with patch_size=4 it yields 49 tokens, which is enough for meaningful self-attention while keeping the parameter count modest. vision_transformer is viable only if patch_size is reduced to 2 (196 tokens) and depth is capped at 4–6 layers; otherwise the token count is too small for the attention mechanism to learn useful relational structure. resnet18 is the least suitable: its stem is designed for 224×224 inputs and will destroy spatial information at 28×28 unless the first conv is replaced with a 3×3 stride-1 kernel. For the 1.63× imbalance, class-weighted cross-entropy or focal loss (γ=1–2) should be the default, and the validation set (10k) is large enough to monitor per-class recall without overfitting to the metric. The cited evidence (efficient transformer design, small-image representation learning) supports the conclusion that at this resolution, inductive bias from convolutional locality outperforms pure attention unless the transformer is explicitly compacted.
parametrization_priorities: Learning rate: start at 1e-3 for CNNs, 3e-4 for transformers; use cosine or step decay with warmup of 5–10 epochs
Weight decay: 1e-4 to 5e-4 for CNNs; 0.05 for transformer (AdamW decoupled)
Batch size: 128–256 for CNNs; 64–128 for transformers (smaller to stabilise attention gradients with few tokens)
Dropout: 0.2–0.3 on classifier head; stochastic depth 0.1–0.2 in residual blocks; avoid heavy dropout in early conv layers at 28×28
Class-weighted loss or focal loss (γ=1.5) to address the 1.63× imbalance; monitor per-class F1 on validation
For transformers: num_heads=4–8, MLP expansion ratio=2–4, num_layers=4–6 (compact) or 8–12 (full ViT); keep d_model ≤ 192 to match the small token count
For CNNs: channel progression 32→64→128→256 with 2–4 residual blocks; kernel size 3×3 throughout
Early stopping patience of 5–8 epochs on validation loss; track both accuracy and macro-F1
representation_priorities: Per-channel normalisation using the provided means [0.7405, 0.5330, 0.7058] and stds [0.1237, 0.1768, 0.1244] before any model input; do not use global mean/std
Preserve full 28×28 spatial resolution through at least the first two feature-extraction stages; avoid stride-2 downsampling before the second block
For transformer variants, use patch_size=4 (49 tokens) as the default; patch_size=2 (196 tokens) only if attention quality is insufficient
Add a lightweight spatial attention or channel-attention (SE-style) module after the second conv block to compensate for the low channel variance and subtle features
Use global average pooling (not max pooling) before the classifier to retain soft spatial information at 28×28
Consider a 1×1 conv 'bottleneck' before the classifier to mix channels without further spatial reduction
If using residual blocks, keep the number of spatial downsampling steps to at most 2 (28→14→7) to retain enough spatial context
Apply data augmentation (random horizontal flip, small rotation ±10°, mild colour jitter) to counteract the low channel variance and reduce overfitting on the 90k samples
risks: Over-parameterisation: resnet18 or a deep ViT on 28×28 images will have more parameters than useful spatial information, leading to overfitting on 90k samples
Token starvation: transformer attention with <50 tokens may degenerate to near-uniform mixing, providing no advantage over a fully-connected layer
Class imbalance masking: overall accuracy may look acceptable while minority-class recall is poor; always track macro-F1 and per-class confusion

Channel variance suppression: the low stds (0.12–0.18) mean that without per-channel normalisation, the model may latch onto the brighter channel (R, mean 0.74) and ignore the more informative G channel (std 0.18)
Premature spatial collapse: any architecture that downsamples below 7×7 before the final pooling loses the spatial detail that 28×28 images carry
Hyperparameter transfer failure: learning rates and weight decay tuned for 224×224 ImageNet-style training will be poorly calibrated for 28×28; re-sweep is mandatory

Validation set leakage risk: with only 10k validation samples and 1.63× imbalance, a few hundred misclassified minority samples can swing the metric; use stratified splits and report confidence intervals
Transformer training instability at low token counts: attention logits can become poorly conditioned with 49 tokens; use pre-norm, gradient clipping (1.0), and a lower peak LR than CNNs
decision.transformer_guidance: At 28×28 the token budget is the binding constraint. With patch_size=4 the sequence length is 49, which is below the typical 196–576 tokens where self-attention learns rich relational structure. Therefore: (a) prefer compact_transformer over vision_transformer—its reduced d_model (64–128) and fewer layers (4–6) are better matched to 49 tokens and the 90k sample budget. (b) If using vision_transformer, set patch_size=2 to obtain 196 tokens, cap depth at 8 layers, d_model=192, heads=6, and add a learnable position embedding (not sinusoidal, since the grid is only 14×14). (c) Add a convolutional stem (2–3 layers of 3×3 conv with stride 2) before the patch embedding to inject local inductive bias; this hybrid 'conv-stem + transformer' pattern is well-supported by the cited efficient-transformer literature and is critical at this resolution. (d) Use LayerNorm (pre-norm) rather than PostNorm for training stability with few tokens. (e) Attention dropout of 0.1 and MLP dropout of 0.1 are sufficient; avoid heavier regularisation that would suppress the already-limited attention signal. (f) Do NOT use resnet18's 7×7 stride-2 stem as a transformer front-end—it destroys 75% of spatial information before the first attention layer. (g) If compute allows, run a small ablation: patch_size 2 vs 4, with and without conv stem, to confirm the token-count hypothesis before committing to a full search.

decision.comment: The architecture_research artefact is internally consistent, well-reasoned, and appropriately scoped for the 28×28×3 PathMNIST task with ~90k training samples and 9 classes. Key consistency checks pass: (1) spatial-resolution analysis correctly identifies the 28→14→7 collapse risk and recommends preserving resolution through at least two stages; (2) token-count arithmetic is correct (patch_size=4 → 49 tokens, patch_size=2 → 196 tokens); (3) channel statistics cited match the data_profile exactly (means [0.7405, 0.5330, 0.7058], stds [0.1237, 0.1768, 0.1244]); (4) imbalance ratio 1.63× matches data_profile; (5) the representation_plan's 'standardize' normalization with train-only stats is consistent with the architecture research's per-channel normalisation recommendation; (6) augmentation_factor=4 in the split_manifest (89996×4=359984) aligns with the augmentation suggestions. The architecture priority ordering (residual_cnn → tiny_cnn → compact_transformer → vision_transformer → resnet18) is well-justified for the resolution constraint. Parametrization ranges (LR, weight decay, batch size, dropout, channel progression) are standard and appropriate for this scale. The risk register correctly identifies over-parameterisation, token starvation, class-imbalance masking, channel-variance suppression, and premature spatial collapse. Minor observations (non-blocking): (a) the source identifier 'qwen3.8' and null llm_model_digest persist from preprocessing—these are provenance concerns, not correctness issues; (b) the risks section could more explicitly flag the external-center domain shift (CRC-VAL-HE-7K) as a design consideration (e.g., domain-adversarial training or stain-normalisation augmentation), though this is more an evaluation-protocol concern than an architecture concern; (c) the known label ambiguities (debris/background, stroma/smooth muscle) are acknowledged in the data_profile but not explicitly referenced in the architecture design rationale. None of these rise to a blocking issue. The artefact is ready to inform downstream model selection and training configuration.

decision.analysis: Round 1 with no prior validation results. The cross-cutting research strongly favours residual_cnn as the primary architecture at 28×28, with compact_transformer as the best transformer entry point (49 tokens at patch_size=4) and tiny_cnn as a fast baseline. Key design decisions: (1) Per-channel standardization is critical given asymmetric channel statistics (means 0.53–0.74, stds 0.12–0.18). (2) Class weighting is enabled for all candidates to address the 1.63× imbalance. (3) Learning rates follow the recommended ranges: ~1e-3 for CNNs, ~3e-4 for transformers. (4) Weight decay is kept low (1e-4) for CNNs and moderate (0.05) for the transformer with AdamW. (5) Augmentations are mild (hflip, rotate90) to avoid destroying subtle spatial features at 28×28. (6) Cosine scheduling with early stopping patience of 5 provides stable convergence. The three candidates span the architecture priority ranking to establish baselines and identify the most promising family before deeper exploration in rounds 2–3.

candidates.rationale: Primary architecture per research priorities. 4 residual blocks with hidden=64 exploit local structure at 28×28 without over-parameterisation. AdamW with cosine decay at lr=1e-3 follows the recommended CNN starting point. Low weight decay (1e-4) avoids over-regularising the subtle channel-variance signal. Class weighting addresses the 1.63× imbalance. Dropout 0.2 on the classifier head provides mild regularisation without suppressing features. Batch 128 balances gradient noise and throughput. Mild augmentations (hflip, rotate90) expand the effective dataset without destroying spatial detail.

Best transformer option at 28×28 per research guidance. patch_size=4 yields 49 tokens—enough for meaningful self-attention while keeping parameters modest. hidden=96 (divisible by num_heads=4, multiple of 8) with 4 layers and mlp_ratio=4 gives a compact but expressive attention model. Lower lr (3e-4) and higher weight decay (0.05) with AdamW follow transformer-specific recommendations. Batch 64 stabilises attention gradients with few tokens. Dropout kept at 0.1 to avoid suppressing the limited attention signal. Learned positional encoding suits the small 7×7 grid. Gradient clipping at 1.0 prevents instability with low token counts.

Fast, low-risk baseline to establish a performance floor and validate hyperparameter choices. hidden=32 with 3 layers keeps the model small and fast to train, enabling quick iteration. Slightly higher lr (2e-3) compensates for the smaller capacity. Larger batch (256) reduces gradient noise for the simpler architecture. Dropout 0.3 provides stronger regularisation appropriate for the smaller model. Three augmentations (hflip, vflip, rotate90) maximise data diversity for the limited capacity. This candidate serves as a reference point: if residual_cnn or compact_transformer do not substantially outperform it, the added complexity is not justified.

decision.analysis: Round 1 established that residual_cnn (hidden=64, depth=4) achieves 98.7% val accuracy, compact_transformer (hidden=96, depth=4) reaches 96.9%, and tiny_cnn (hidden=32, depth=3) hits 96.6%. The residual CNN is clearly the strongest architecture at 28×28. For round 2, I will: (1) push the residual CNN to its maximum allowed hidden width (96) with slightly more depth (5) and a marginally lower LR to exploit the extra capacity without overfitting; (2) scale up the compact transformer to hidden=128, depth=6, mlp_ratio=3, and switch to mean pooling to better aggregate the 49-token sequence; (3) introduce a vision_transformer with patch_size=2 (196 tokens) to test whether more tokens meaningfully improve attention quality at this resolution. All three use standardize normalization, class weighting for the 1.63× imbalance, and cosine scheduling. Weight decay is kept conservative (≤0.05) to avoid over-regularising the already-subtle channel signals (stds 0.12–0.18).

candidates.rationale: Round-1 residual_cnn (hidden=64, depth=4) scored 98.7% val accuracy. This candidate widens hidden to the 96 cap for residual_cnn, adds one more residual block (depth=5) for richer feature hierarchy, slightly lowers LR (8e-4 vs 1e-3) to stabilise the wider network, and reduces label smoothing to 0.05 since the model is already well-calibrated. Dropout is trimmed to 0.15 to let the extra width carry more signal. Weight decay nudged to 2e-4 for mild L2 regularisation without suppressing the low-variance channel features.

Round-1 compact_transformer (hidden=96, depth=4, cls pooling) reached 96.9%. This candidate increases hidden to 128 (divisible by 4 heads, multiple of 8), deepens to 6 layers for more sequential context mixing over the 49 tokens, reduces mlp_ratio to 3 to keep parameter count in check, and switches to mean pooling which is more robust than cls-token pooling when the sequence is short. LR raised to 5e-4 to compensate for the deeper network. Weight decay at 0.03 (AdamW decoupled) provides moderate regularisation. Batch size increased to 128 for more stable gradient estimates with the larger model.

Testing the token-count hypothesis: patch_size=2 yields 196 tokens (vs 49 at patch_size=4), giving self-attention 4× more relational structure to exploit. Hidden=128 with 4 heads (32-dim per head) keeps the model compact. Depth capped at 4 to avoid overfitting on 90k samples. LR kept at 3e-4 (transformer-appropriate) with AdamW and 0.05 weight decay for decoupled regularisation. Batch size 64 stabilises attention gradients with the longer sequence. Three augmentations (hflip, vflip, rotate90) maximise effective training diversity. This is the highest-risk candidate but tests whether the compact_transformer's 96.9% ceiling is due to token starvation.

decision.analysis: Round 3 (final). The best validation result so far is res_cnn_wide_d5 (hidden=96, depth=5, val_acc=0.987505). The constraint now caps residual_cnn hidden at 96, so I will push depth to 6 with a slightly lower LR to stabilise the extra block, and add brightness augmentation to exploit the low channel variance. For the second slot, I explore the compact_transformer with patch_size=2 (196 tokens) to test whether more tokens close the ~1.8pp gap to the CNN, keeping the best transformer settings (mean pooling, mlp_ratio=3, hidden=128, depth=6) from compact_tf_d6_mean.

candidates.rationale: Extends the best CNN (res_cnn_wide_d5, 0.9875) by adding one more residual block (depth 6) while keeping hidden at the 96 cap. Lower LR (6e-4 vs 8e-4) compensates for the extra depth to avoid instability. Dropout raised to 0.2 for the deeper stack. Brightness augmentation added to counteract the low channel stds (0.12-0.18) and reduce overfitting on the 90k samples. Cosine schedule and AdamW with 2e-4 weight decay match the prior best configuration.

Tests the token-count hypothesis: patch_size=2 yields 196 tokens (vs 49 at patch_size=4), giving self-attention 4x more relational structure to exploit. LR 4e-4 is between the two prior transformer LRs. Weight decay 0.03 (AdamW decoupled) regularises the larger attention matrices. decision.comment:
Model search stage is complete and internally consistent. Key observations:

1. **Search completeness**: All 8 planned trials completed with 0 failures. Architecture coverage spans residual_cnn (3 variants), compact_transformer (3 variants), tiny_cnn (1), and vision_transformer (1), providing adequate exploration of the design space identified in the architecture research.
